summary: Joan of Arc is the best-documented commoner of the Middle Ages, but nearly everything we know comes from two church trials that each set out to prove a verdict. This profile tests how the template handles rich but partisan evidence.

active_period.display: 221–190 BCE as a commander; Italy 218–203 BCE

summary: Hannibal is one of the most famous commanders in history, yet not one line of Carthaginian history about him survives. Everything comes from Greek and Roman writers on the winning side, so this profile tests how the database handles a record that is detailed but almost entirely hostile.

Sundiata founded the Mali Empire in the 13th century, but almost everything about him comes from the oral epic performed by Mande griots and recorded only in the 20th century. This profile tests whether the database can respect oral tradition as evidence without treating its every episode as fact.

Sun Tzu is the reverse of Hannibal: his book is one of the best-preserved military texts in the world, but the man himself may barely have existed. This profile tests a figure whose importance lies in a text, not a battle record.

active_period.display: c. 1800s–1849; leader of the migration south from c. 1820

cultural_guidance: Ka Mate is a taonga of Ngāti Toa Rangatira, who are its kaitiaki (Haka Ka Mate Attribution Act 2014). Do not reproduce the words of Ka Mate in quizzes or games. Knowledge held by Ngāti Toa and by the other iwi in this story should be used only as the iwi have placed it in the public record; Te Rūnanga o Toa Rangatira is the right authority for the Ngāti Toa perspective, and anything sensitive should follow the iwi's own guidance.
summary: Te Rauparaha led Ngāti Toa from near-destruction at Kāwhia to the conquest of much of central New Zealand, and composed the haka Ka Mate. He is remembered very differently by Ngāti Toa, by the iwi his forces defeated, and by colonial writers, so this profile tests how the database holds several legitimate perspectives at once.

cultural_guidance: Revered in Mongolia as the father of the nation; describe his reputation there with respect alongside the record of conquest.
summary: Genghis Khan united the peoples of the Mongolian steppe and launched the conquests that created the largest contiguous land empire in history. His life is known mainly from one anonymous Mongol chronicle and from the histories of peoples he conquered or employed, so nearly every source has a stake in how he is remembered.

Subutai served three Mongol khans and fought from northern China to Hungary, yet he is a shadowy figure as a person. His biography survives only in Chinese translation, and much of what is popularly said about him is modern invention. This profile tests how the database handles a famous name whose popular image has run far ahead of the evidence.

cultural_guidance: A national and religious hero in Egypt, Syria and Kazakhstan; record his reputation there respectfully alongside the record of violence.
summary: Baibars was a Kipchak Turk enslaved as a boy who became sultan of Egypt and Syria, fought at the battle that first stopped the Mongols in the Middle East, and reduced the crusader states to a strip of coast. He reached the throne by murdering his sultan. This profile tests how the database handles a ruler celebrated by court biographers, a folk epic and modern nations, and condemned by his enemies.

cultural_guidance: Worshipped as a deity, Đức Thánh Trần, at temples across Vietnam; describe the cult respectfully and keep it separate from claims about the historical man.
summary: Trần Hưng Đạo was a prince of Vietnam's Trần dynasty who led Đại Việt's resistance to the Mongol-Yuan invasions of the 1280s, ending with the destruction of a Yuan fleet at the Bạch Đằng River in 1288. He is now revered in Vietnam both as a national hero and as a deity. This profile tests how the database handles a figure whose modern image was shaped by nationalism, and whose popular history is full of inflated numbers.

cultural_guidance: A national hero in Uzbekistan; record that status respectfully alongside the victims' memory.
summary: Timur set out to rebuild the Mongol Empire without being descended from Genghis Khan, and came close: from the 1370s to his death in 1405 he campaigned from Delhi to Ankara and from Damascus to the steppes north of the Caspian. He is remembered for the destruction of cities and for the culture his dynasty created in Samarkand and Herat. This profile tests how the database handles a conqueror who manufactured his own legitimacy, down to (probably) his birth date.
